answerBody:
A state should be able to condition public preschool funding on compliance with equal-opportunity enrollment rules, even when some religious providers decline the funds. The governing default is conditional inclusion, not a right to public money plus an exemption from the program's defining rule. St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, argued November 3, 2026, and still undecided, does not change that judgment.

Colorado's universal preschool program, launched in 2023, offers families up to 15 hours of free preschool each week at participating providers. Participation requires an agreement to give eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability, including as those traits apply to a child's family. Faith-based providers may teach their faith. They may not take the money and refuse families because of sexual orientation or gender identity. The Archdiocese of Denver and affiliated Catholic preschools want an exemption so they can enroll only families open to Catholic teaching on marriage, sex, and gender. A unanimous Tenth Circuit, in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, No. 24-1267 (Sept. 30, 2025), held the condition neutral and generally applicable under Employment Division v. Smith (1990) and rationally related to equal access. SCOTUSblog's case page states the questions as whether Smith requires unfettered discretion or identical secular exemptions, and whether Carson v. Makin (2022) applies only to explicit religious exclusion. Amy Howe's November 3, 2026 argument analysis reported that a majority seemed inclined toward stricter review or a remand. Inclination is not a holding.

The better frame separates religious status and instruction from publicly funded admissions. Trinity Lutheran, Espinoza, and Carson forbid excluding schools because they are religious or teach religion. Colorado does neither. It asks every funded provider, secular or religious, to keep funded seats open. Declining funds is not exclusion from civic life. It is refusal of a subsidy whose purpose is universal access. Judge Richard Federico's opinion captured the point: when a school takes money meant to ensure universal education, its doors must be open to all. Disability and low-income preferences do not undermine that rule. They enlarge access. An exclusionary preference contracts it.

The strongest counterargument is that a condition known to be unacceptable to some faiths is exclusion in practical effect, and that Sherbert v. Verner (1963) protects believers even under formally neutral benefit rules. Oral argument pressed that comparison, and a future majority may adopt it. That extension should be rejected. Sherbert involved an individual denied benefits for observing a Sabbath, not a provider seeking public tuition while closing funded seats to protected families. If effect alone triggers strict scrutiny, any civil-rights condition that some religion rejects becomes presumptively unconstitutional. States could not define a universal program as universal.

Uncertainty remains because the Court may narrow Smith or expand Carson before June 2027. Until it does, public preschool money should follow open enrollment. Religious providers keep their creed, their private admissions, and their freedom to decline the subsidy.

Conditional inclusion is defended from the Tenth Circuit's September 30, 2025 holding, SCOTUSblog's statement of the questions, and Amy Howe's November 3, 2026 argument analysis, while distinguishing Carson, Trinity Lutheran, and Espinoza from a generally applicable open-enrollment condition and rejecting a Sherbert-style effects extension. The case remains undecided, and that uncertainty is stated. The word-counting capability confirmed answerBody is within range.
